reductions.name: Provability over RCA₀*
reductions.description: Implication provable over RCA₀*, i.e. RCA₀ with Σ⁰₁-induction replaced by Δ⁰₀-induction and the totality of exponentiation (Simpson–Smith 1986).

reductions.name: Provability over RCA₀
reductions.description: Implication provable over the base system RCA₀.

reductions.name: ω-model implication
reductions.phrase: every ω-model of {a} is a model of {b}
reductions.description: Every ω-model (equivalently every Turing ideal) satisfying the first statement satisfies the second.

reductions.name: Strong Weihrauch reduction
reductions.description: There are Turing functionals Φ, Ψ such that for every instance X of the second problem, Φ(X) is an instance of the first, and for every solution Y of Φ(X), Ψ(Y) is a solution of X (Ψ has no access to X).

reductions.name: Weihrauch reduction
reductions.description: Uniform reduction: Φ maps instances to instances, Ψ maps (original instance, solution) to solutions.

reductions.name: Strong computable reduction
reductions.description: Every instance X of the second problem computes an instance X̂ of the first such that every solution of X̂ computes a solution of X.

reductions.name: Computable reduction
reductions.description: Every instance X of the second problem computes an instance X̂ of the first such that for every solution Ŷ of X̂, X ⊕ Ŷ computes a solution of X.

reductions.name: Generalized Weihrauch reduction
reductions.description: Uniform reduction allowing finitely many adaptive uses of the first problem (Hirschfeldt–Jockusch 2016).

properties.name: Cone avoidance
properties.description: For every set Z and every C ≰_T Z, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that C ≰_T Z ⊕ Y.

properties.name: PA avoidance
properties.description: For every set Z which is not of PA degree, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that Z ⊕ Y is not of PA degree.

properties.name: Low basis
properties.description: For every Z, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that (Z ⊕ Y)' ≤_T Z'.

properties.name: Weakly low basis
properties.description: For every Z, every set P of PA degree over Z′ and every Z-computable instance, there is a solution Y such that (Y ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T P (Liu–Patey 2026 and Patey–Shafer 2026, Definition 3.2). It implies the low₂ basis by the low basis theorem relative to Z′.

properties.name: Low₂ basis
properties.description: For every Z, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that (Y ⊕ Z)″ ≤_T Z″.

properties.name: Weakly low₂ basis
properties.description: For every Z, every set P of PA degree over Z″ and every Z-computable instance, there is a solution Y such that (Y ⊕ Z)″ ≤_T P. It implies the low₃ basis.

properties.name: Δ⁰₂ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Δ⁰₂ solution.

properties.name: Σ⁰₂ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Σ⁰₂ solution.

properties.name: Π⁰₂ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Π⁰₂ solution.

properties.name: Δ⁰₃ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Δ⁰₃ solution.

properties.name: Σ⁰₃ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Σ⁰₃ solution.

properties.name: Π⁰₃ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Π⁰₃ solution.

properties.name: Σ⁰₄ basis
properties.description: Every computable instance has a Σ⁰₄ solution.

properties.name: Computably true
properties.description: Every instance X has a solution computable in X. Equivalently, the problem holds in every ω-model (Turing ideal), i.e. RCA₀ implies it over ω-models: so NON, DNR, WKL… fail it, and the engine reads it off the ω-model comparison with RCA₀.

properties.name: Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀
properties.description: RCA₀ + the statement proves no Π¹₁ sentence which is not already provable in RCA₀.

properties.name: Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂
properties.description: RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂ + the statement proves no Π¹₁ sentence which is not already provable in RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂. Principles weaker than RT²₂ (COH, ADS, CAC, EM…) have it; whether RT²₂ does was a long-standing question.

properties.name: Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀ + IΣ⁰₂
properties.description: RCA₀ + IΣ⁰₂ + the statement proves no Π¹₁ sentence which is not already provable in RCA₀ + IΣ⁰₂ (Cholak, Jockusch and Slaman for RT²₂).

properties.name: Preservation of hyperimmunity (countably many sets)
properties.description: For every set Z and every countable collection A₀, A₁, … of Z-hyperimmune sets, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that every Aᵢ is (Z ⊕ Y)-hyperimmune (Patey, "Iterative forcing and hyperimmunity in reverse mathematics", Definition 4.2; Patey's thesis, Definition 6.2.1). Preserving finitely many hyperimmune sets is weaker: RT²₂ preserves one but not two.

properties.name: Preservation of k hyperimmunities for every k
properties.description: For every k ∈ ω, every set Z and Z-hyperimmune sets A₀, …, A_{k−1}, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that every Aᵢ is (Z ⊕ Y)-hyperimmune (Patey's thesis, Definition 6.2.2, for every k). The free set and thin set theorems have it.

properties.name: Preservation of 3 hyperimmunities
properties.description: For every set Z and Z-hyperimmune sets A₀, A₁, A₂, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A₀, A₁, A₂ are (Z ⊕ Y)-hyperimmune (Patey's thesis, Definition 6.2.2, k = 3). TS²₄ has it and STS²₃ fails it.

properties.name: Preservation of 2 hyperimmunities
properties.description: For every set Z and Z-hyperimmune sets A₀, A₁, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A₀ and A₁ are (Z ⊕ Y)-hyperimmune (Patey's thesis, Definition 6.2.2, k = 2). TS²₃ has it; SRT²₂, SADS and ADS fail it. Not to be confused with the preservation of 2-hyperimmunity of Liu and Patey.

properties.name: Preservation of one hyperimmunity
properties.description: For every set Z and Z-hyperimmune set A, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A is (Z ⊕ Y)-hyperimmune (Patey's thesis, Definition 6.2.2, k = 1). RT²₂ has it.

properties.name: Preservation of Δ⁰₂ definitions
properties.description: For every Z and every set A which is not Δ⁰₂(Z), every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A is not Δ⁰₂(Z ⊕ Y) (Wang).

properties.name: Preservation of the arithmetic hierarchy
properties.description: For every Z, every n, and every set A which is not Σ⁰ₙ(Z) (resp. Π⁰ₙ, Δ⁰ₙ), every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A is still not Σ⁰ₙ(Z ⊕ Y) (resp. Π⁰ₙ, Δ⁰ₙ).

properties.name: Preservation of c.b.-immunity
properties.description: For every Z and every set A which is computably bounded immune relative to Z, every Z-computable instance has a solution Y such that A is c.b.-immune relative to Z ⊕ Y (Patey, "Partial orders and immunity").

properties.name: Preservation of dependent hyperimmunity
properties.description: Preservation of dependent hyperimmunity, in the sense of Patey, "Partial orders and immunity in reverse mathematics".

properties.name: Preservation of 2-hyperimmunity (Liu–Patey)
properties.description: Preservation of 2-hyperimmunity in the sense of Liu and Patey, "The reverse mathematics of the thin set and Erdős–Moser theorems": for every set C and every C-2-hyperimmune pair, every C-computable instance has a solution G relative to which the pair is still 2-hyperimmune.

properties.name: Cylinder
properties.description: id × P ≤sW P (Definition 3.4 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly). Equivalently, every problem Weihrauch reducible to P is strongly Weihrauch reducible to it (Proposition 3.5); compositional products are cylinders (Proposition 5.4), and so are jumps of cylinders (Proposition 6.14).

properties.name: Strongly parallelizable
properties.description: P̂ ≡sW P (Definition 4.2 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly).

properties.name: Parallelizable
properties.description: P̂ ≡W P (Definition 4.2 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly). A parallelizable problem is idempotent (Proposition 4.4).

properties.name: Closed under compositional product
properties.description: P ⋆ P ≤W P. Then P × P ≤W P ⋆ P ≤W P, so P is idempotent; P⋄ is the least problem above P closed under compositional product.

properties.name: Idempotent
properties.description: P × P ≡W P (Definition 4.2 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly).

properties.name: Finitely tolerant
properties.description: Weihrauch equivalent to some P :⊆ ℕ^ℕ ⇒ ℕ^ℕ with a computable T such that for inputs p, q that agree from position k on, every solution r of q gives a solution T⟨r, k⟩ of p (Definition 4.5 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly, after Dorais, Dzhafarov, Hirst, Mileti and Shafer). Every jump is finitely tolerant (Proposition 6.13).

properties.name: Fractal
properties.description: Weihrauch equivalent to some F :⊆ ℕ^ℕ ⇒ ℕ^ℕ with F restricted to A ≡W F for every clopen A meeting the domain of F (Definition 4.10 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly). Fractals are countably irreducible (Proposition 4.11); every jump is a strong fractal (Proposition 6.13).

properties.name: Countably irreducible
properties.description: P ≤W ⊔ᵢ Qᵢ implies P ≤W Qᵢ for some i, for every sequence of problems (Definition 4.9 of Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly). It implies join-irreducibility.

properties.name: Join-irreducible
properties.description: P ≤W Q ⊔ R implies P ≤W Q or P ≤W R (Brattka, Gherardi and Pauly, Section 4).

statements.label: \mathsf{CL}_{\mathrm{c}}
statements.name: Cousin's lemma for continuous gauges
statements.definition: For every continuous gauge $\delta : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^+$ there is a $\delta$-fine tagged partition of $[0,1]$.

statements.label: \mathsf{CL}_{\mathrm{B1}}
statements.name: Cousin's lemma for Baire class 1 gauges
statements.definition: Cousin's lemma restricted to gauges of Baire class 1.

statements.label: \mathsf{UKT}
statements.name: Uniform Kruskal theorem
statements.definition: The uniform Kruskal theorem of Freund, Rathjen and Weiermann: a uniform version of Kruskal's theorem for recursive data types given by normal transformations of well partial orders.

statements.label: \mathsf{TLPP}
statements.name: Transfinite leftmost path principle
statements.definition: Towsner's transfinite leftmost path principle: an axiom asserting the existence of leftmost paths through ill-founded trees, relative to hyperarithmetic hierarchies along well-orders. The theory $\mathsf{TLPP}_0$ ($\mathsf{RCA}_0$ + TLPP) lies between $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ and $\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}_0$.

statements.label: \mathsf{JD}
statements.name: Jordan decomposition theorem
statements.definition: Every function $f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$ of bounded variation is the difference of two non-decreasing functions.

statements.label: \mathsf{JD}_{\mathrm{c}}
statements.name: Jordan decomposition theorem (continuous)
statements.definition: Every continuous function of bounded variation on $[0,1]$ is the difference of two continuous non-decreasing functions.

statements.label: \mathsf{BV}\text{-}\mathsf{DIFF}
statements.name: Differentiability of BV functions
statements.definition: Every function of bounded variation on $[0,1]$ is differentiable almost everywhere.

statements.label: \mathsf{ART}^2_2
statements.name: Ramsey theorem for additive colourings
statements.definition: Ramsey's theorem for pairs restricted to additive colourings (colourings into a finite semigroup with $c(i,k) = c(i,j) \cdot c(j,k)$), asserting an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to S$ into a finite semigroup with $c(i,k) = c(i,j) \cdot c(j,k)$.
statements.solution: An infinite homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{BC}
statements.name: Büchi's complementation theorem
statements.definition: Every language recognized by a nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a complement recognized by a nondeterministic Büchi automaton.

statements.label: \mathsf{FPT}
statements.name: Fishburn's possibility theorem
statements.definition: Fishburn's possibility theorem for countable societies: there is a social welfare function satisfying Arrow's conditions.

statements.label: \mathsf{AHT}
statements.name: Adjacent Hindman's theorem
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to k$ there is an infinite set $H = \{h_1 < h_2 < \dots\}$ such that all sums of finitely many consecutive elements $h_i + h_{i+1} + \dots + h_j$ have the same color (with the apartness condition on the binary expansions of the $h_i$).
statements.instance: A finite coloring of $\mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set whose finite sums of adjacent elements are monochromatic.

statements.label: \mathsf{HIL}
statements.name: Hilbert's theorem
statements.definition: Variant of Hindman's theorem studied by Hirst, equivalent to the infinite pigeonhole principle; see the source.

statements.label: \mathsf{FIN}_k
statements.name: Gowers' FIN_k theorem
statements.definition: Gowers' pigeonhole principle for $\mathrm{FIN}_k$, a generalization of Hindman's theorem.
statements.instance: A number $k$ and a finite coloring of $\mathrm{FIN}_k$.
statements.solution: An infinite block sequence whose generated combinatorial subspace is monochromatic.

statements.label: \mathsf{AP}
statements.name: Existence of almost periodic points
statements.definition: Every continuous map on a compact metric space has an almost periodic point.

statements.label: \mathsf{ACA}^+
statements.name: ω-th jump
statements.definition: For every $X$, the $\omega$-th jump $X^{(\omega)}$ exists.
statements.instance: A set $X$.
statements.solution: The $\omega$-th jump $X^{(\omega)}$.

statements.label: \mathsf{ACA}'
statements.name: Finite jumps
statements.definition: For every $n$ and every $X$, the $n$-th jump $X^{(n)}$ exists.
statements.instance: A set $X$ and a number $n$.
statements.solution: The $n$-th jump $X^{(n)}$.

statements.label: \mathsf{WOP}(\varepsilon_X)
statements.name: Well-ordering principle for ε
statements.definition: If $X$ is a well-ordering, then so is $\varepsilon_X$.

statements.label: \mathsf{BRD}_{\mathbb{H}}
statements.name: Finite big Ramsey degrees of Henson graphs
statements.definition: The Henson graphs have finite big Ramsey degrees.

statements.label: \mathsf{CPT}\Rightarrow\mathsf{LEB}
statements.name: Compact spaces are Lebesgue
statements.definition: Every compact metric space is Lebesgue: every open covering has a Lebesgue number.

statements.label: \mathsf{BROOKS}
statements.name: Brooks' theorem
statements.definition: Brooks' theorem for arbitrary countable graphs: a connected graph of maximum degree $d \ge 3$ other than $K_{d+1}$ is $d$-colorable.

statements.label: \mathbf{3}\text{-}\mathsf{BQO}
statements.name: The antichain with three elements is bqo
statements.definition: The discrete order with three elements is a better quasi-order.

statements.label: \mathsf{INV}
statements.name: Brouwer invariance theorems
statements.definition: Brouwer's invariance of dimension and domain theorems (in the formulations of Kihara 2020).

statements.label: \mathsf{EVP}
statements.name: Ekeland's variational principle
statements.definition: Ekeland's variational principle for lower semicontinuous functions on complete separable metric spaces.

statements.label: \mathsf{SCT}
statements.name: Size-change termination criterion
statements.definition: The size-change termination criterion of Lee, Jones and Ben-Amram.

statements.label: \mathsf{TET}
statements.name: Tietze extension theorem
statements.definition: Versions of the Tietze extension theorem for functions with moduli of uniform continuity.

statements.label: \mathsf{HST}
statements.name: Helly's selection theorem
statements.definition: Every bounded sequence of functions of bounded variation has a subsequence converging in the weak* topology.

statements.label: \mathsf{TT}
statements.name: Tree theorem for all exponents
statements.definition: For every $n$ and $k$, the tree theorem $\mathsf{TT}^n_k$ holds.
statements.instance: Numbers $n, k$ and a coloring of the $n$-element chains of $2^{<\mathbb{N}}$ with $k$ colors.
statements.solution: A homogeneous subtree isomorphic to $2^{<\mathbb{N}}$.

statements.label: \mathsf{PR}^2
statements.name: Packed Ramsey theorem for pairs
statements.definition: $\mathsf{PRT}^2_k$: for every $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $w \to (\varphi(w))^2_{k+1}$ for all $w$, and every $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to \{1, \dots, k\}$, there is a set $H$ which is packed for $\varphi$ and semi-homogeneous for $f$ (Erdős–Galvin).
statements.instance: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $w \to (\varphi(w))^2_{k+1}$ for all $w$, and a coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to \{1, \dots, k\}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set packed for $\varphi$ and semi-homogeneous for $f$.

statements.label: \mathsf{HB}
statements.name: Hahn–Banach theorem (separable)
statements.definition: Every bounded linear functional on a closed subspace of a separable Banach space extends to the whole space with the same norm.
statements.instance: A separable Banach space, a closed subspace and a bounded functional on it.
statements.solution: A norm-preserving extension of the functional.
statements.caution: The acronyms HB and HBT name the Hahn–Banach theorem in some papers and the Heine–Borel covering lemma ([[heine-borel]]) in others: check the definition in each paper.

statements.label: \mathsf{FRA}
statements.name: Fraïssé's conjecture (Laver's theorem)
statements.definition: The countable linear orders are well-quasi-ordered under embeddability: for every sequence $(L_n)$ of countable linear orders there are $i < j$ such that $L_i$ embeds into $L_j$.

statements.label: \mathsf{NWT}
statements.name: Nash-Williams' theorem on transfinite sequences
statements.definition: If $Q$ is a better quasi-order and $\alpha$ is a countable well-order, then the set $S_\alpha(Q)$ of $\alpha$-sequences of elements of $Q$, ordered by embeddability, is a better quasi-order.

statements.label: \mathsf{NWT}_{\mathrm{fin}}
statements.name: Nash-Williams' theorem for sequences with finite range
statements.definition: If $Q$ is a well-quasi-order and $\alpha$ is a countable well-order, then the set of $\alpha$-sequences of elements of $Q$ with finite range, ordered by embeddability, is a well-quasi-order.

statements.label: \mathsf{GHT}
statements.name: Generalized Higman theorem
statements.definition: If $Q$ is a better quasi-order, then so is the set $Q^{<\omega}$ of finite sequences of elements of $Q$ under embeddability.

statements.label: \mathsf{AET}
statements.name: Auslander–Ellis theorem
statements.definition: For every point $x$ of a compact dynamical system $(X, T)$ there is a uniformly recurrent point $y$ which is proximal to $x$.

statements.label: \mathsf{VDW}
statements.name: Van der Waerden's theorem
statements.definition: For every finite coloring of $\mathbb{N}$, some color class contains arbitrarily long finite arithmetic progressions.

statements.label: \mathsf{BL}
statements.name: Brown's lemma
statements.definition: Every finite coloring $C : \mathbb{N} \to r$ has a homogeneous piecewise syndetic set, i.e. a homogeneous set that, for some $d$, contains arbitrarily large finite sets whose consecutive elements differ by at most $d$.

statements.label: \mathsf{RL}
statements.name: Rudin's lemma
statements.definition: Given a countable poset $(X, \preceq)$ and a $\preceq$-directed family $(F_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty finite subsets of $X$, there is a $\preceq$-directed subset $D \subseteq \bigcup_i F_i$ that meets every $F_i$.

statements.label: \mathsf{MTT}
statements.name: Milliken's tree theorem
statements.definition: Let $T$ be an infinite tree with no leaves. For all $n, k \ge 1$ and every coloring $f : S_n(T) \to k$ of the strong subtrees of $T$ of height $n$, there is a strong subtree $S$ of $T$ of height $\omega$ such that $f$ is constant on $S_n(S)$.

statements.label: \mathsf{MTT}^2
statements.name: Milliken's tree theorem for height 2
statements.definition: Milliken's tree theorem restricted to colorings of the strong subtrees of height 2.

statements.label: \mathsf{MTT}^3
statements.name: Milliken's tree theorem for height 3
statements.definition: Milliken's tree theorem restricted to colorings of the strong subtrees of height 3.

statements.label: \mathsf{HL}
statements.name: Halpern–Läuchli theorem
statements.definition: For infinite trees $T_0, \dots, T_{d-1}$ with no leaves and every $k$-coloring of $\bigcup_n T_0(n) \times \dots \times T_{d-1}(n)$, there are strong subtrees $S_0, \dots, S_{d-1}$ with a common level function such that the coloring is constant on $\bigcup_n S_0(n) \times \dots \times S_{d-1}(n)$. It is the product Milliken tree theorem for height 1.
statements.instance: Infinite bounded trees $T_0, \dots, T_{d-1}$ with no leaves and a coloring $f : \bigcup_n T_0(n) \times \dots \times T_{d-1}(n) \to k$.
statements.solution: Strong subtrees $(S_0, \dots, S_{d-1}) \in S_\omega(T_0, \dots, T_{d-1})$ on whose level product $f$ is constant.

statements.label: \mathsf{PMTT}
statements.name: Product Milliken tree theorem
statements.definition: For infinite trees $T_0, \dots, T_{d-1}$ with no leaves, all $n, k$ and every $f : S_n(T_0, \dots, T_{d-1}) \to k$, there is $(S_0, \dots, S_{d-1}) \in S_\omega(T_0, \dots, T_{d-1})$ such that $f$ is constant on $S_n(S_0, \dots, S_{d-1})$.

statements.label: \mathsf{PMTT}^2
statements.name: Product Milliken tree theorem for height 2
statements.definition: The product version of Milliken's tree theorem restricted to colorings of strong subtree products of height 2.

statements.label: \mathsf{DT}^2
statements.name: Devlin's theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every $k$ and every $f : [\mathbb{Q}]^2 \to k$ there is a dense suborder $S \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ without endpoints with $|f([S]^2)| \leq 2$ (that is, $(\forall k)\,\mathsf{DT}^2_{k,2}$; the bound 2 is optimal, as observed by Galvin).

statements.label: \mathsf{RG}^2
statements.name: Rado graph theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every $k$ and every coloring $f : [R]^2 \to k$ of the pairs of the Rado graph $R$, there is a subgraph $R' \subseteq R$ isomorphic to $R$ with $|f''[R']^2| \leq 4$ (that is, $(\forall k)\,\mathsf{RG}^2_{k,4}$).

statements.label: \mathsf{BCG}\text{-}\mathsf{Det}
statements.name: Determinacy of binary choice games
statements.definition: Every clopen game on integers in which each player has at most two possible moves at each turn (a well-founded binary choice game tree) is determined.

statements.label: \mathsf{MLE}
statements.name: Maximal linear extension theorem
statements.definition: Every well partial order has a linear extension of maximal order type (de Jongh and Parikh).

statements.label: \mathsf{RCA}_0^*
statements.name: Weak recursive comprehension
statements.definition: Δ⁰₁ comprehension together with Δ⁰₀ induction and the totality of exponentiation (Simpson–Smith 1986). It is the base theory of the reduction "provability over RCA₀*", and is implied by every statement over RCA₀* , RCA₀ and ω-models.
statements.context: RCA₀* was introduced by Simpson and Smith [@simpsonsmith1986] to study theorems of algebra under weak induction. It replaces Σ⁰₁-induction by Δ⁰₁-induction together with the totality of exponentiation. Over RCA₀*, RCA₀ itself becomes a statement like the others (it is equivalent to IΣ⁰₁), and principles that are equivalent over RCA₀ may split according to how much induction they need.

statements.label: \mathsf{RCA}_0
statements.name: Recursive comprehension
statements.definition: Δ⁰₁ comprehension together with Σ⁰₁ induction. It is the usual base system of reverse mathematics, and hence implied by every statement over RCA₀ and over ω-models. Over the weaker base theory RCA₀* it is a genuine statement, equivalent to Σ⁰₁ induction.
statements.context: RCA₀ is the usual base theory of reverse mathematics [@friedman1975] [@simpson2009]: Δ⁰₁-comprehension with Σ⁰₁-induction. Its ω-models are exactly the Turing ideals, so a statement holds in all ω-models of RCA₀ when every instance computed by a set has a solution computable from it. A good part of computable mathematics — the intermediate value theorem, the algebraic closure of a countable field, … — is provable in RCA₀. Over the weaker RCA₀* it is equivalent to IΣ⁰₁.

statements.label: \mathsf{WKL}
statements.name: Weak König's lemma
statements.definition: Every infinite subtree of $2^{<\mathbb{N}}$ has an infinite path.
statements.instance: An infinite binary tree $T \subseteq 2^{<\mathbb{N}}$.
statements.solution: An infinite path through $T$.
statements.context: Weak König's lemma is the second of the Big Five [@simpson2009]. Over RCA₀ it is equivalent to many compactness arguments of ordinary mathematics: the Heine–Borel covering lemma for [0,1], Gödel's completeness theorem, the Brouwer fixed point theorem, the Hahn–Banach theorem for separable spaces, the existence of prime ideals in countable commutative rings. Its solutions are paths through binary trees, i.e. members of Π⁰₁ classes; by the low basis theorem [@jockuschsoare1972] every computable instance has a low solution. It is Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀. In the Weihrauch lattice it is the parallelization of LLPO [@brattkagherardi2011].

statements.label: \Sigma^0_1\text{-}\mathsf{SEP}
statements.name: Σ⁰₁ separation
statements.definition: For every pair of disjoint $\Sigma^0_1$ sets $A, B$, there is a set $S$ with $A \subseteq S$ and $S \cap B = \emptyset$.
statements.instance: Two disjoint $\Sigma^0_1$ sets $A$, $B$ (given by enumerations).
statements.solution: A set $S$ separating $A$ from $B$.

statements.label: \mathsf{WWKL}
statements.name: Weak weak König's lemma
statements.definition: Every binary tree $T$ of positive measure, i.e. $\lim_s |T \cap 2^s| / 2^s > 0$, has an infinite path.
statements.instance: A binary tree of positive measure.
statements.solution: An infinite path through it.
statements.context: Weak weak König's lemma restricts WKL to binary trees of positive measure. Yu and Simpson [@yusimpson1990] introduced it and showed that it is strictly weaker than WKL; it is the natural setting for measure theory in reverse mathematics. Over RCA₀ it amounts to the existence, relative to every set, of a Martin-Löf random set, and it implies DNR [@giustosimpson2000].

statements.label: \mathsf{DNR}
statements.name: Diagonally non-recursive functions
statements.definition: For every set $X$, there is a function $f$ such that $f(e) \neq \Phi^X_e(e)$ for every $e$.
statements.instance: A set $X$.
statements.solution: A function $f$ which is diagonally non-computable relative to $X$.
statements.context: DNR asserts that relative to every set there is a diagonally non-recursive function. It is implied by WWKL [@giustosimpson2000] — every Martin-Löf random set computes a DNR function [@kucera1985] — and strictly weaker than it [@ambosspiesetal2004]. It is also a consequence of SRT²₂ [@hirschfeldtetal2008], and is the computability-theoretic core of many Ramsey-type principles: over RCA₀ it is equivalent to the Ramsey-type weak weak König's lemma [@bienvenupateyshafer2017].

statements.caution: ACA₀ is equivalent over RCA₀ to the existence of Turing jumps, but as problems they differ: ACA here receives an arithmetical formula with a set parameter and returns the set it defines, while the jump X ↦ X′ is [[tj]], which unlike ACA has the Δ⁰₂ basis property.
statements.label: \mathsf{ACA}
statements.name: Arithmetical comprehension
statements.definition: Every set defined by an arithmetical formula exists. Equivalently over RCA₀, every set has a Turing jump (the problem form of the jump is TJ).
statements.instance: A set $X$ and an arithmetical formula $\varphi(n, X)$.
statements.solution: The set $\{n : \varphi(n, X)\}$.
statements.context: ACA₀, the third of the Big Five, adds comprehension for arithmetical formulas; over RCA₀ it is equivalent to the existence of the Turing jump of every set. It is equivalent to König's lemma [@friedman1975], the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, the existence of bases of countable vector spaces and of maximal ideals of countable commutative rings, and to Ramsey's theorem RTⁿ₂ for every fixed n ≥ 3 [@jockusch1972] [@simpson2009]. Its first-order part is Peano arithmetic.

statements.caution: Equivalent to ACA₀ over RCA₀, but not the same problem as ACA ([[aca]]), which returns the set defined by an arbitrary arithmetical formula with a set parameter.
statements.label: \mathsf{TJ}
statements.name: Turing jump
statements.definition: Every set has a Turing jump. As a problem: given $X$, compute $X'$ (the map $J$ of Weihrauch complexity, strongly Weihrauch equivalent to $\lim$). Over RCA₀ it is equivalent to ACA₀.
statements.instance: A set $X$.
statements.solution: The Turing jump $X'$.

statements.caution: In the Weihrauch lattice, ATR names a problem (Definition 3.12 of [@kiharamarconepauly2020]) that is strongly Weihrauch equivalent to [[ucnn]] (Theorem 3.13), not to closed choice [[cnn]]; its two-sided version is [[atr2]]. The results here about ATR concern the axiom ATR₀.
statements.label: \mathsf{ATR}
statements.name: Arithmetical transfinite recursion
statements.definition: Arithmetical comprehension can be iterated along any countable well-ordering.
statements.context: ATR₀, the fourth of the Big Five, asserts that arithmetical operators can be iterated along any countable well-ordering. Over RCA₀ it is equivalent to the comparability of countable well-orderings, the perfect set theorem for closed sets, Lusin's separation theorem and Ulm's theorem [@simpson2009]. It is the natural home of predicative mathematics beyond ACA₀.

statements.label: \Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}
statements.name: Π¹₁ comprehension
statements.definition: Every set defined by a $\Pi^1_1$ formula exists.
statements.context: Π¹₁-CA₀ is the strongest of the Big Five: every Π¹₁ formula defines a set, equivalently every set has a hyperjump. Over RCA₀ it is equivalent to the Cantor–Bendixson theorem and to the decomposition of every countable abelian group as the direct sum of a divisible group and a reduced group [@simpson2009].

statements.label: \textsf{SS}
statements.name: Every set belongs to a countable Scott set
statements.definition: Every set belongs to a countable (coded) Scott set: a nonempty family closed under join, in which every infinite binary tree computable from a member has an infinite path in the family.

statements.label: \mathsf{I}\Sigma^0_1
statements.name: Σ⁰₁ induction
statements.definition: The induction scheme restricted to $\Sigma^0_1$ formulas.

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ collection
statements.definition: For every $\Sigma^0_2$ formula $\varphi$ and every $n$: if $\forall i < n\, \exists y\, \varphi(i, y)$ then there is a bound $b$ with $\forall i < n\, \exists y < b\, \varphi(i, y)$.
statements.context: Σ⁰₂-collection sits strictly between IΣ⁰₂ and IΣ⁰₁ in the hierarchy of Paris and Kirby [@pariskirby1978], and is Π⁰₃-conservative over RCA₀ [@paris1980]. It is equivalent over RCA₀ to the infinite pigeonhole principle RT¹_{<∞} [@hirst1987] and to Δ⁰₂-induction [@slaman2004]. Many Ramsey-type principles imply it, which makes it the usual yardstick for their first-order strength.

statements.label: \mathsf{I}\Delta^0_2
statements.name: Δ⁰₂ induction
statements.definition: The induction scheme restricted to $\Delta^0_2$ formulas.

statements.label: \mathsf{I}\Sigma^0_2
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ induction
statements.definition: The induction scheme restricted to $\Sigma^0_2$ formulas.

statements.label: \mathsf{SRT}^2_3
statements.name: Stable Ramsey's theorem for pairs (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{ADC}
statements.name: Ascending or descending chain
statements.caution: For strong Weihrauch reducibility the domain of the instance matters. Here the linear order has domain ℕ, as in Astor et al. [@astoretal2017]; Fiori-Carones, Shafer and Soldà [@fioricaronesshafersolda2022] allow any infinite subset of ℕ, which gives the cylindrification of this problem (same Weihrauch degree). Their strong reductions and cylinder claims are about that version.
statements.definition: Every infinite linear order has an infinite ascending chain or an infinite descending chain (as sets, without the order of enumeration).
statements.instance: An infinite linear order.
statements.solution: An infinite set which is an ascending chain or a descending chain.

statements.caution: Hindman's theorem is also called the finite sums theorem; FS here is the free set theorem ([[fs]]).
statements.label: \mathsf{HT}
statements.name: Hindman's theorem
statements.definition: For every finite coloring of $\mathbb{N}$ there is an infinite set $H$ such that all nonempty finite sums of distinct elements of $H$ have the same color.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to k$.
statements.solution: An infinite set all of whose finite sums have the same color.

statements.label: \mathsf{HT}^{\le 3}_3
statements.name: Hindman's theorem for sums of at most 3 elements (3 colors)
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 3$ there is an infinite set $H$ such that all sums of at most 3 distinct elements of $H$ have the same color.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{HT}^{\le 2}_2
statements.name: Hindman's theorem for sums of at most 2 elements
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 2$ there is an infinite set $H$ such that all sums of at most 2 distinct elements of $H$ have the same color.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{HT}^{=2}_2
statements.name: Hindman's theorem for sums of exactly 2 elements
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 2$ there is an infinite set $H$ such that all sums of exactly 2 distinct elements of $H$ have the same color.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : \mathbb{N} \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSg}
statements.name: Rival–Sands theorem for graphs
statements.caution: For strong Weihrauch reducibility the vertex set matters. Here, as in Fiori-Carones, Shafer and Soldà [@fioricaronesshafersolda2022], it is any infinite subset of ℕ; this version is the cylindrification of the one with vertex set ℕ (their Proposition 7.2), and both have the same Weihrauch degree.
statements.definition: Every infinite graph $G$ contains an infinite subset $H$ such that every vertex of $G$ is adjacent to none, exactly one, or infinitely many vertices of $H$.
statements.instance: An infinite graph $G$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSgr}
statements.name: Rival–Sands theorem for graphs, refined
statements.definition: Every infinite graph $G = (V, E)$ contains an infinite $H \subseteq V$ such that every vertex of $G$ has infinitely many or at most one neighbours in $H$, and every vertex of $H$ has infinitely many or no neighbours in $H$.
statements.instance: An infinite graph $G$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{wRSgr}
statements.name: Weak Rival–Sands theorem for graphs, refined
statements.definition: Every infinite graph $G = (V, E)$ contains an infinite $H \subseteq V$ such that every vertex of $H$ has infinitely many or no neighbours in $H$.
statements.instance: An infinite graph $G$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSpo}
statements.name: Rival–Sands theorem for partial orders of finite width
statements.definition: Every infinite partial order $P$ of finite width contains an infinite chain $C$ such that every element of $P$ is comparable with no element or with infinitely many elements of $C$.
statements.instance: An infinite partial order of finite width.
statements.solution: An infinite chain $C$ as above.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSpo}_3
statements.name: Rival–Sands theorem for partial orders of width at most 3
statements.definition: The Rival–Sands theorem restricted to partial orders of width at most 3.
statements.instance: An infinite partial order of width at most 3.
statements.solution: An infinite chain $C$ such that every element is comparable with no element or with infinitely many elements of $C$.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSpo}_{\mathrm{CD}}
statements.name: Rival–Sands theorem for unions of two chains
statements.definition: The Rival–Sands theorem restricted to partial orders decomposable into two chains.
statements.instance: An infinite partial order which is a union of two chains.
statements.solution: An infinite chain $C$ such that every element is comparable with no element or with infinitely many elements of $C$.

statements.label: \mathsf{ERT}
statements.name: Eventually constant Ramsey-type principle
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$ there is $b$ such that every color appearing after $b$ appears at least twice after $b$: for all $x \ge b$ there is $y \ge b$ with $y \ne x$ and $f(x) = f(y)$.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$.
statements.solution: A number $b$ such that every color appearing after $b$ appears at least twice after $b$.

statements.label: \mathsf{ECT}
statements.name: Eventually constant tail principle
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$ there is $b$ such that every color appearing after $b$ appears infinitely often (eventually constant palette tail).
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$.
statements.solution: A number $b$ such that every color appearing after $b$ appears infinitely often.

statements.label: \mathsf{W}2\text{-}\mathsf{RAN}
statements.name: Existence of weakly 2-randoms
statements.definition: For every $Z$ there is a set which is weakly 2-random relative to $Z$.
statements.instance: A set $Z$.
statements.solution: A set weakly 2-random relative to $Z$.

statements.caution: CR abbreviates computable randomness in randomness papers, and closed choice on the reals ([[cr]]) in Weihrauch papers.
statements.label: \mathsf{CR}\text{-}\mathsf{RAN}
statements.name: Existence of computable randoms
statements.definition: For every $Z$ there is a set which is computably random relative to $Z$.
statements.instance: A set $Z$.
statements.solution: A set computably random relative to $Z$.

statements.label: \mathsf{SR}\text{-}\mathsf{RAN}
statements.name: Existence of Schnorr randoms
statements.definition: For every $Z$ there is a set which is Schnorr random relative to $Z$.
statements.instance: A set $Z$.
statements.solution: A set Schnorr random relative to $Z$.

statements.label: \mathsf{BRT}^2_2
statements.name: Bounded Ramsey's theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ whose 1-homogeneous sets have bounded size, there is an infinite 0-homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring whose 1-homogeneous sets are of bounded size.
statements.solution: An infinite 0-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{BRT}^3_2
statements.name: Bounded Ramsey's theorem for triples
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^3 \to 2$ whose 1-homogeneous sets have bounded size, there is an infinite 0-homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring of triples whose 1-homogeneous sets are of bounded size.
statements.solution: An infinite 0-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{BRT}^4_2
statements.name: Bounded Ramsey's theorem for quadruples
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^4 \to 2$ whose 1-homogeneous sets have bounded size, there is an infinite 0-homogeneous set. Unlike $\mathsf{BRT}^2_2$ and $\mathsf{BRT}^3_2$, it is equivalent to $\mathsf{ACA}_0$.
statements.instance: A coloring of quadruples whose 1-homogeneous sets are of bounded size.
statements.solution: An infinite 0-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{OVW}
statements.name: Ordered variable word theorem
statements.definition: For every finite alphabet $A$ and finite coloring of the words over $A$, there is a word $c_0$ and an infinite sequence of left-variable words $w_1, w_2, \dots$ such that all words $c_0 \cdot w_1[a_1] \cdots w_k[a_k]$ have the same color.
statements.instance: A finite alphabet $A$ and a finite coloring of $A^{<\mathbb{N}}$.
statements.solution: A word $c_0$ and an infinite sequence of left-variable words as in the statement.

statements.label: \mathsf{fin}\text{-}\mathsf{COH}
statements.name: Finite cohesiveness principle
statements.definition: COH restricted to finite sequences of sets.
statements.instance: A finite sequence of sets $R_0, \dots, R_{n-1}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $C$ with $C \subseteq^* R_i$ or $C \subseteq^* \overline{R_i}$ for each $i < n$.

statements.label: \mathsf{CAC}\text{ for trees}
statements.name: CAC for trees
statements.caution: Not the tree antichain theorem TAC of Conidis ([[ctac]]), which only concerns completely branching c.e. binary trees and is strictly weaker: CAC for trees is equivalent to TAC + BΣ⁰₂ (Theorem 2.5 of [@cervellegaudelierpatey2022]).
statements.definition: Every infinite subtree of $\mathbb{N}^{<\mathbb{N}}$ has an infinite path or an infinite antichain.
statements.instance: An infinite subtree $T$ of $\mathbb{N}^{<\mathbb{N}}$.
statements.solution: An infinite path of $T$ or an infinite antichain of $T$.

statements.label: \mathsf{TAC}
statements.name: Tree antichain theorem (Conidis)
statements.caution: Not CAC for trees ([[tac]]), which is equivalent to TAC + BΣ⁰₂ (Theorem 2.5 of [@cervellegaudelierpatey2022]); TAC does not imply BΣ⁰₂.
statements.definition: Every infinite completely branching $\Sigma^0_1$-definable (c.e.) tree $T \subseteq 2^{<\mathbb{N}}$ has an infinite antichain; completely branching: if $\sigma i \in T$ then $\sigma(1-i) \in T$.
statements.instance: An infinite completely branching c.e. tree $T \subseteq 2^{<\mathbb{N}}$.
statements.solution: An infinite antichain of $T$.

statements.label: \mathsf{IND}_{\mathcal{H}_3}
statements.name: Indivisibility of the triangle-free Henson graph
statements.definition: For every 2-coloring of the vertices of the universal countable triangle-free (Henson) graph, there is a monochromatic set of vertices inducing a copy of the whole graph.
statements.instance: A 2-coloring of the vertices of the triangle-free Henson graph.
statements.solution: A monochromatic set of vertices inducing a copy of the graph.

statements.label: \mathsf{SADC}
statements.name: Stable ascending or descending chain
statements.definition: Every infinite stable linear order has an infinite ascending chain or an infinite descending chain (a chain need not be a sequence in the order of $\mathbb{N}$, unlike for SADS).
statements.instance: An infinite stable linear order $L$.
statements.solution: An infinite $C \subseteq L$ which is an ascending chain or a descending chain of $L$.

statements.label: \mathsf{wRSg}
statements.name: Weak Rival–Sands theorem for graphs
statements.caution: For strong Weihrauch reducibility the vertex set matters. Here, as in Fiori-Carones, Shafer and Soldà [@fioricaronesshafersolda2022], it is any infinite subset of ℕ; this version is the cylindrification of the one with vertex set ℕ (their Proposition 7.2), and both have the same Weihrauch degree.
statements.definition: For every infinite graph $G = (V, E)$ there is an infinite $H \subseteq V$ such that for every $x \in H$, either $H \cap N(x)$ is infinite or $|H \cap N(x)| \le 1$.
statements.instance: An infinite graph $G = (V, E)$.
statements.solution: An infinite $H \subseteq V$ such that every $x \in H$ has either infinitely many or at most one neighbour in $H$.

statements.label: \mathsf{MMLC}
statements.name: Maximal max-less chain principle
statements.definition: Every partial order has a max-less chain (a chain with no maximum element) which is $\subseteq$-maximal among the max-less chains.

statements.label: \mathsf{NFP}
statements.name: Noetherian rings have finitely many prime ideals
statements.caution: In higher-order reverse mathematics, NFP is the neighbourhood function principle, an unrelated statement about functionals (Definition 5.1 of [@sanders2019b]); it is not in the catalogue.
statements.definition: Every Noetherian ring has only finitely many prime ideals.

statements.label: \Delta^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}
statements.name: Δ¹₁ comprehension
statements.definition: Comprehension for $\Delta^1_1$-definable sets: if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are $\Sigma^1_1$ formulas with $(\forall n)[\varphi(n) \leftrightarrow \neg\psi(n)]$, then $\{n : \varphi(n)\}$ exists. HYP is its minimum $\omega$-model.

statements.label: \mathsf{IHT}
statements.name: Iterated Hindman's theorem
statements.definition: For every sequence of 2-colorings $\langle C_i : i \in \mathbb{N} \rangle$ there is an increasing sequence $\langle x_i \rangle$ such that for every $j$, the set $\{x_i : i > j\}$ satisfies Hindman's theorem for $C_j$. Equivalent over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ to AUF and to the Milliken–Taylor theorem $\mathsf{MT}^n$ for $n \ge 3$, and over $\mathsf{ACA}_0$ to the Auslander–Ellis theorem.

statements.caution: In Weihrauch and computability papers this problem is usually written PA; here PA ([[pa]]) is first-order Peano arithmetic, the full induction scheme.
statements.label: \textsf{PA degrees}
statements.name: PA degrees (problem)
statements.definition: Given $p$, find $q$ of PA degree relative to $p$ ($p \ll q$).
statements.instance: A set $p$.
statements.solution: A set $q$ with $p \ll q$, i.e. of PA degree relative to $p$.

statements.label: \Sigma^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{AC}
statements.name: Σ¹₁ axiom of choice
statements.definition: $\mathsf{ACA}_0$ plus the scheme $\forall n \exists Y \eta(n, Y) \to \exists Z \forall n \eta(n, (Z)_n)$ for $\Sigma^1_1$ formulas $\eta$. Strictly between $\Delta^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}_0$ and $\mathsf{ATR}_0$; HYP is an $\omega$-model of it.

statements.label: \mathsf{CAC}^{\mathrm{ord}}
statements.name: Chain–antichain principle for ω-ordered partial orders
statements.definition: Every infinite $\omega$-ordered partial order ($x \le_P y$ implies $x \le y$) has an infinite chain or antichain.
statements.instance: An infinite $\omega$-ordered partial order $(P, \le_P)$.
statements.solution: An infinite chain or antichain of $P$.

statements.label: \mathsf{SCAC}^{\mathrm{ord}}
statements.name: Stable chain–antichain principle for ω-ordered partial orders
statements.definition: Every infinite $\omega$-ordered stable partial order has an infinite $\omega$-ordered chain or antichain.
statements.instance: An infinite $\omega$-ordered stable partial order $(P, \le_P)$.
statements.solution: An infinite chain or antichain of $P$.

statements.label: 2\text{-}\mathsf{SDNR}
statements.name: Stable diagonal non-computability
statements.definition: Every $\Delta^0_2$ function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ has an $f$-diagonalizing function, i.e. a function $g$ with $g(x) \neq f(x)$ for every $x$. A characterization of $\mathsf{SRRT}^2_2$.
statements.instance: A $\Delta^0_2$ function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, given by an approximation $h$ with $f(x) = \lim_s h(x, s)$.
statements.solution: A function $g$ with $g(x) \neq f(x)$ for every $x$.

statements.label: \mathsf{RSAT}_{\text{2-branching}}
statements.name: Ramsey-type satisfiability for 2-branching clauses
statements.definition: $\mathsf{RSAT}$ restricted to 2-branching sets of clauses over atoms $\{a_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$: in every clause $\ell_0 \vee \dots \vee \ell_{n-1}$, each literal $\ell_i$ is $a_i$ or $\neg a_i$.
statements.instance: A finitely satisfiable 2-branching set $C$ of clauses.
statements.solution: An infinite set of atoms homogeneous for $C$.

statements.label: \Sigma^0_2\textsf{-separation}
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ separation principle
statements.definition: For every two disjoint $\Sigma^0_2$ sets $A_0, A_1$ (with set parameters) there is a $\Delta^0_2$ set $D$ with $A_0 \subseteq D$ and $D \cap A_1 = \emptyset$. Equivalent to $\mathsf{COH}$ over $\mathsf{RCA}_0 + \mathrm{B}\Sigma^0_2$.

statements.label: \mathsf{PH}
statements.name: Paris–Harrington principle
statements.definition: For all $n, k, l$ there is $u$ such that for every finite set $X$ of size at least $u$, every $k$-coloring of $[X]^n$ has a homogeneous set $H$ of size at least $l$ with $\min H \geq |H|$. An arithmetic sentence, true but not provable in Peano arithmetic.

statements.label: \mathsf{EXT}(\omega^*)
statements.name: Well-ordered linear extensions
statements.definition: Every countable well-founded partial order has a well-ordered linear extension (the order type $\omega^*$ is weakly extendible).

statements.label: \mathsf{EXT}(\zeta)
statements.name: Weak extendibility of ζ
statements.definition: Every countable partial order with no linear suborder of type $\zeta$ (the integers) has a linear extension with no suborder of type $\zeta$.

statements.label: \textsf{Dushnik–Miller}
statements.name: Dushnik–Miller theorem (countable linear orders)
statements.definition: Every countable infinite linear order has a nontrivial self-embedding (an order-preserving map into itself that is not the identity).
statements.instance: A countable infinite linear order $L$.
statements.solution: A nontrivial self-embedding of $L$.

statements.label: \textsf{Strongly atomic trees}
statements.name: Atomic trees are strongly atomic
statements.definition: Every atomic binary tree with no dead ends is strongly atomic. A node $\sigma$ is an atom if it has exactly one extension of each length; the tree is atomic if every node extends to an atom, and strongly atomic if for all $\sigma_0, \dots, \sigma_n$ in the tree, each $\sigma_i$ extends to an atom.

statements.label: \textsf{finite-}\Sigma^1_1\textsf{-AC}_0
statements.name: Σ¹₁ axiom of finite choice
statements.definition: For every arithmetic $\varphi(n, Y)$: if for each $n$ there are finitely many $Y$ with $\varphi(n, Y)$, then there is a sequence $(Z_n)_n$ with $\varphi(n, Z_n)$ for every $n$ (implicitly, at least one $Y$; equivalently, a sequence of trees with finitely many paths has a sequence of paths). A theory of hyperarithmetic analysis.

statements.label: \mathsf{ABW}_0
statements.name: Arithmetic Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem
statements.definition: For every arithmetic predicate $A(X)$ on $2^\mathbb{N}$, either $A$ has finitely many solutions or the set $\{X \in 2^\mathbb{N} : A(X)\}$ has an accumulation point.

statements.label: \mathsf{IRT}
statements.name: Infinite ray theorem (Halin)
statements.definition: If a graph $G$ has, for each $k$, a set of $k$ disjoint rays, then it has an infinite set of disjoint rays. A natural theorem of hyperarithmetic analysis.

statements.label: \mathsf{WIRT}
statements.name: Weak infinite ray theorem
statements.definition: If $G$ is a graph and $(X_k)_k$ is a sequence such that each $X_k$ is a set of $k$ disjoint rays of $G$, then $G$ has an infinite set of disjoint rays.

statements.label: \mathsf{DOM}
statements.name: Domination principle
statements.definition: Every weakly represented family of functions has a function dominating it, i.e. eventually greater than each member; equivalently, for every set $C$ there is a function dominating every $C$-computable function. In ω-models, this is the existence of sets of high degree relative to any set (Martin).
statements.instance: A set $C$.
statements.solution: A function $g$ dominating every $C$-computable function.

statements.label: \mathsf{AVOID}
statements.name: Avoidance principle
statements.definition: Every weakly represented family of functions has a function eventually different from each member; equivalently, for every set $C$ there is a function eventually different from every $C$-computable function.
statements.instance: A set $C$.
statements.solution: A function $g$ eventually different from every $C$-computable function.

statements.label: \mathsf{BI}
statements.name: Bi-immunity principle
statements.definition: For every weakly represented family of infinite sets there is a set $B$ such that no member is contained in $B$ or in its complement; equivalently, for every set $C$ there is a set which is bi-immune relative to $C$.
statements.instance: A set $C$.
statements.solution: A set $B$ such that neither $B$ nor its complement contains an infinite $C$-computable set.

statements.label: \mathsf{PM}
statements.name: Perfect matching theorem (Steffens)
statements.definition: Every countable graph satisfying condition (A) (for every matching $M$ and every vertex outside $M$ there is an $M$-augmenting path starting at it) has a perfect matching.

statements.label: \mathsf{MM}
statements.name: Maximal matching theorem (Steffens)
statements.definition: Every countable graph has a matching whose support is not properly contained in the support of another matching.

statements.label: \mathsf{MIM}
statements.name: Maximal independent matching
statements.definition: Every countable graph has an independent matching whose support is not properly contained in the support of another independent matching.

statements.label: \exists k \forall f\, \mathsf{DNR}(k, f)
statements.name: Uniformly bounded DNR
statements.definition: There is a $k$ such that for every $f$ there is a $k$-bounded function which is diagonally non-recursive relative to $f$.

statements.label: \forall f \exists k\, \mathsf{DNR}(k, f)
statements.name: Non-uniformly bounded DNR
statements.definition: For every $f$ there are a $k$ and a $k$-bounded function which is diagonally non-recursive relative to $f$.

statements.label: \mathsf{VEL}
statements.name: Valuation extension lemma
statements.definition: For every Kripke frame $(W, R)$ and every assignment $v : W \times \mathrm{Prop} \to 2$ of the propositional variables, there is a valuation on $(W, R)$ (a truth value for every modal formula at every world, respecting the clauses of the connectives and of $\Box$) extending $v$.

statements.label: \mathsf{VEL}_{\mathrm{res}}
statements.name: Restricted valuation extension lemma
statements.definition: For every Kripke frame $(W, R)$, assignment $v$ and $k$, there is a $k$-restricted valuation (defined on the formulas of modal degree at most $k$) extending $v$.

statements.label: \textsf{Countable bounded Banach}
statements.name: Countable bounded Banach theorem
statements.definition: For injections $f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ whose ranges exist, there is a bijection $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $h(n) = m$ implies $f(n) = m$ or $g(m) = n$ (the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein argument of Banach).

statements.label: \textsf{Milliken}
statements.name: Milliken's theorem (block sums)
statements.caution: Not Milliken's tree theorem ([[mtt]]), which colors strong subtrees.
statements.definition: For each $n$, every finite coloring of the $n$-tuples of block sums has an infinite set $X$ such that all $n$-tuples $\{\sum A_0, \dots, \sum A_{n-1}\}$ with $A_i$ finite subsets of $X$ and $\max A_i < \min A_j$ for $i < j$ have the same color. For $n = 1$ it is Hindman's theorem.

statements.label: \mathsf{MIRT}
statements.name: Maximal infinite ray theorem
statements.definition: Every graph has a (possibly finite) sequence of disjoint rays which is maximal: no ray of the graph is disjoint from all of them (for each of the variants of graphs, disjointness and rays of the infinite ray theorem).

statements.label: \mathsf{CAC}
statements.name: Chain–antichain principle
statements.definition: Every infinite partial order has an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.
statements.instance: An infinite partial order $(\mathbb{N}, \preceq)$.
statements.solution: An infinite chain or an infinite antichain.
statements.context: The chain/antichain principle: every infinite partial order has an infinite chain or antichain. It follows from RT²₂ and implies ADS [@hirschfeldtshore2007]; Hirschfeldt and Shore showed that it does not imply DNR, so it is far from RT²₂ computationally. It is Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂ [@chongslamanyang2012].

statements.label: \mathsf{SCAC}
statements.name: Stable chain–antichain principle
statements.definition: Every infinite stable partial order has an infinite chain or an infinite antichain.
statements.instance: An infinite stable partial order.
statements.solution: An infinite chain or an infinite antichain.

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence
statements.caution: For strong Weihrauch reducibility the domain of the instance matters. Here the linear order has domain ℕ, as in Astor et al. [@astoretal2017]; Fiori-Carones, Shafer and Soldà [@fioricaronesshafersolda2022] allow any infinite subset of ℕ, which gives the cylindrification of this problem (same Weihrauch degree). Their strong reductions and cylinder claims are about that version.
statements.definition: Every infinite linear order has an infinite ascending or an infinite descending sequence.
statements.instance: An infinite linear order $(\mathbb{N}, <_L)$.
statements.solution: An infinite ascending or descending sequence.
statements.context: The ascending/descending sequence principle: every infinite linear order has an infinite ascending or descending sequence. Hirschfeldt and Shore [@hirschfeldtshore2007] studied it with CAC as consequences of RT²₂ that are neither computably true nor strong enough to imply DNR; ADS implies COH and is strictly weaker than CAC [@lermansolomontowsner2013]. It is Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂ [@chongslamanyang2012].

statements.label: \mathsf{SADS}
statements.name: Stable ascending or descending sequence
statements.definition: Every infinite linear order of type $\omega + \omega^*$ has an infinite ascending or descending sequence.
statements.instance: An infinite linear order of type $\omega + \omega^*$.
statements.solution: An infinite ascending or descending sequence.

statements.label: \mathsf{CADS}
statements.name: Cohesive ascending or descending sequence
statements.definition: Every infinite linear order has a stable suborder, i.e. an infinite suborder of type $\omega$, $\omega^*$ or $\omega + \omega^*$.
statements.instance: An infinite linear order.
statements.solution: An infinite stable suborder.

statements.label: \mathsf{TRT}^2_2
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for transitive colorings
statements.definition: Every transitive coloring of pairs with 2 colors (each color class is a transitive relation on pairs $x < y$) has an infinite homogeneous set. Equivalent to ADS.
statements.instance: A transitive coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{MC}
statements.name: Maximal chain theorem for well partial orders
statements.definition: Every well partial order $P$ has a chain $C$ such that every chain of $P$ embeds into $C$ (Wolk's theorem).

statements.label: \mathsf{WRT}^2
statements.name: Weak Ramsey theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every $k$ and every $P : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to k$ there are a color $c$ and an infinite set $\{x_0 < x_1 < \dots\}$ with $P(x_i, x_{i+1}) = c$ for all $i$. With two colors it is psRT²₂, equivalent to ADS.

statements.label: \textsf{Termination Theorem}
statements.name: Podelski–Rybalchenko termination theorem
statements.definition: A binary relation $R$ is well-founded if there are $k$ well-founded relations whose union contains the transitive closure of $R$ (a disjunctively well-founded transition invariant).

statements.label: \textsf{H-closure Theorem}
statements.name: H-closure theorem
statements.definition: The union of finitely many H-well-founded relations is H-well-founded.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^1_2
statements.name: Infinite pigeonhole principle (2 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 2$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ on which $f$ is constant.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^1_3
statements.name: Infinite pigeonhole principle (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 3$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ on which $f$ is constant.

statements.caution: For Weihrauch reducibility it matters whether the number of colors is part of the instance: here the bound k is given, unlike RT¹_ℕ ([[rt1n]]) of Goh, Pauly and Valenti [@gohpaulyvalenti2021]. Check which convention a paper uses.
statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^1_{<\infty}
statements.name: Infinite pigeonhole principle (finitely many colors)
statements.definition: For every $k$, every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A number $k$ and a coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to k$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ on which $f$ is constant.
statements.context: The infinite pigeonhole principle: every finite coloring of ℕ has an infinite monochromatic set. Over RCA₀ it is equivalent to BΣ⁰₂ [@hirst1987]. Under Weihrauch reducibility, where the number of colors is part of the instance, it is a genuinely non-trivial problem studied together with its fixed-color versions RT¹ₖ.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^2_2
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for pairs
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ such that $f$ is constant on $[H]^2$.
statements.context: Ramsey's theorem for pairs and two colors [@ramsey1930] is the most studied principle of the zoo. Jockusch [@jockusch1972] showed that computable colorings have Π⁰₂ but not necessarily Σ⁰₂ (in particular not necessarily computable) solutions; Seetapun [@seetapunslaman1995] showed that RT²₂ admits cone avoidance and therefore does not imply ACA₀. Cholak, Jockusch and Slaman [@cholakjockuschslaman2001] decomposed it into SRT²₂ + COH and showed it is Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀ + IΣ⁰₂. Liu [@liu2012] proved that it does not imply WKL. Whether SRT²₂ implies it remained open for a long time: Chong, Slaman and Yang [@chongslamanyang2014] separated them with a non-standard model, and Monin and Patey [@moninpatey2021] in ω-models. Over RCA₀ it is also equivalent to EM + ADS [@bovykinweiermann2017].

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^2_3
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for pairs (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ such that $f$ is constant on $[H]^2$.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^3_2
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for triples
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^3 \to 2$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^3 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ such that $f$ is constant on $[H]^3$.

statements.label: \mathsf{SRT}^2_2
statements.name: Stable Ramsey's theorem for pairs
statements.definition: Every stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ (i.e. $\lim_y f(x, y)$ exists for every $x$) has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ such that $f$ is constant on $[H]^2$.
statements.context: Stable Ramsey's theorem for pairs restricts RT²₂ to colorings in which every element eventually has a fixed color with all larger elements. By the limit lemma it is equivalent over RCA₀ to D²₂, the statement that every Δ⁰₂ set has an infinite subset contained in it or in its complement [@cholakjockuschslaman2001] [@chonglemppyang2010]; the two formulations come apart under finer reductions [@dzhafarov2016]. It is strictly weaker than RT²₂ [@chongslamanyang2014] [@moninpatey2021], and does not imply IΣ⁰₂ [@chongslamanyang2014].

statements.label: \mathsf{D}^2_2
statements.name: Δ⁰₂ subset principle
statements.definition: For every stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ there is an infinite set $H$ and a color $i$ such that $\lim_y f(x, y) = i$ for all $x \in H$. Equivalently, every $\Delta^0_2$ set has an infinite subset in it or its complement.
statements.instance: A stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set which is limit-homogeneous for $f$.

statements.label: \mathsf{COH}
statements.name: Cohesiveness principle
statements.definition: For every sequence of sets $R_0, R_1, \dots$, there is an infinite set $C$ such that for every $i$, either $C \subseteq^* R_i$ or $C \subseteq^* \overline{R_i}$.
statements.instance: A sequence of sets $\vec R$.
statements.solution: An infinite $\vec R$-cohesive set.
statements.context: Cohesiveness asks, for a sequence of sets R₀, R₁, …, for an infinite set C that is, for each i, almost contained in Rᵢ or in its complement. Cholak, Jockusch and Slaman [@cholakjockuschslaman2001] isolated it as the "unstable" half of RT²₂ (RT²₂ ⇔ SRT²₂ + COH) and showed it Π¹₁-conservative over RCA₀. A set computes solutions to all computable instances exactly when its jump is PA relative to ∅′ [@jockuschstephan1993]; in particular COH admits no low basis. In ω-models it is independent of SRT²₂ in both directions: COH does not even imply DNR [@hirschfeldtetal2008], and SRT²₂ does not imply COH [@moninpatey2021].

statements.label: \mathsf{EM}
statements.name: Erdős–Moser theorem
statements.definition: Every infinite tournament has an infinite transitive subtournament.
statements.instance: An infinite tournament $T$ on $\mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ on which $T$ is transitive.
statements.context: The Erdős–Moser theorem: every tournament on ℕ has an infinite transitive subtournament. It follows from RT²₂, and together with ADS it is equivalent to RT²₂ over RCA₀ [@bovykinweiermann2017]. Lerman, Solomon and Towsner [@lermansolomontowsner2013] showed that it implies neither SRT²₂ nor ADS, even over ω-models.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^1_4
statements.name: Infinite pigeonhole principle (4 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 4$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 4$.
statements.solution: An infinite set on which $f$ is constant.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^1_5
statements.name: Infinite pigeonhole principle (5 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 5$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 5$.
statements.solution: An infinite set on which $f$ is constant.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^4_2
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for quadruples
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^4 \to 2$ has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^4 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ such that $f$ is constant on $[H]^4$.

statements.label: \mathsf{TS}^2_3
statements.name: Thin set theorem for pairs (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$ has an infinite set $H$ that is thin for $f$, i.e. $f$ avoids at least one color on $[H]^2$.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[[H]^2] \neq 3$.

statements.label: \mathsf{TS}^2_4
statements.name: Thin set theorem for pairs (4 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 4$ has an infinite set $H$ such that $f$ avoids at least one color on $[H]^2$.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 4$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[[H]^2] \neq 4$.

statements.label: \mathsf{STS}^2_3
statements.name: Stable thin set theorem for pairs (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$ (for every $x$, $\lim_s f(x, s)$ exists) has an infinite set $H$ such that $f$ avoids at least one color on $[H]^2$.
statements.instance: A stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[[H]^2] \neq 3$.

statements.label: \mathsf{STS}^2_4
statements.name: Stable thin set theorem for pairs (4 colors)
statements.definition: Every stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 4$ has an infinite set $H$ such that $f$ avoids at least one color on $[H]^2$.
statements.instance: A stable coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 4$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[[H]^2] \neq 4$.

statements.label: \mathsf{TS}^1_3
statements.name: Thin set theorem for singletons (3 colors)
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 3$ has an infinite set $H$ such that $f$ avoids at least one color on $H$. Every computable instance has a computable solution; the principle is studied for strong computable reducibility, where it lies strictly below $\mathsf{RT}^1_2$.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : \mathbb{N} \to 3$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[H] \neq 3$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{RT}^2_2
statements.name: Long Ramsey's theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ there exists a set $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ (the range of a strictly increasing map with domain $\mathbb{N}$) such that $c$ is constant on $[H]^2$. Over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ it is $\mathsf{RT}^2_2$; over $\mathsf{RCA}_0^*$ it implies $\mathrm{I}\Sigma^0_1$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{RT}^3_2
statements.name: Long Ramsey's theorem for triples
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^3 \to 2$ there exists a set $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ such that $c$ is constant on $[H]^3$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{CAC}
statements.name: Long chain–antichain principle
statements.definition: For every partial order $(\mathbb{N}, \preceq)$ there exists a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ which is either a chain or an antichain.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{ADS}_{\mathrm{set}}
statements.name: Long ascending or descending sequence (set solutions)
statements.definition: For every linear order $(\mathbb{N}, \preceq)$ there exists a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ on which $\preceq$ agrees with $\leq$, or on which $\preceq$ agrees with $\geq$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{ADS}_{\mathrm{seq}}
statements.name: Long ascending or descending sequence (sequence solutions)
statements.definition: For every linear order $(\mathbb{N}, \preceq)$ there exists a sequence $(s_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ which is either strictly $\preceq$-increasing or strictly $\preceq$-decreasing.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{CRT}^2_2
statements.name: Long cohesive Ramsey theorem for pairs
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ there exists a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ such that for each $x \in S$ there is $y \in S$ with $c(x, z) = c(x, y)$ for all $z \in S$ with $z \geq y$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{COH}
statements.name: Long cohesiveness principle
statements.definition: For every sequence $(R_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ there is a set $C$ of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ which is cohesive for $(R_n)_n$.

statements.label: \ell\text{-}\mathsf{EM}
statements.name: Long Erdős–Moser theorem
statements.definition: For every coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ there is a set of cardinality $\mathbb{N}$ on which $c$ is transitive.

statements.label: \mathsf{TS}
statements.name: Thin set theorem
statements.definition: For every $n$, every function $f : [\mathbb{N}]^n \to \mathbb{N}$ has an infinite thin set $H$, i.e. $f[[H]^n] \neq \mathbb{N}$.
statements.instance: A number $n$ and a function $f : [\mathbb{N}]^n \to \mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set $H$ with $f[[H]^n] \neq \mathbb{N}$.

statements.label: \mathsf{SHER}
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for semi-hereditary colorings
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ which is semi-hereditary for some color $i$ (for all $x < y < z$, $f(x, z) = f(y, z) = i$ implies $f(x, y) = i$) has an infinite homogeneous set. Equivalent to CAC for trees.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ semi-hereditary for some color.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-homogeneous set.

refs.loc: Definitions 6.1 and 6.2 (introduced by Dorais et al.)

statements.label: \mathsf{HEM}
statements.name: Half Erdős–Moser theorem
statements.definition: For every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ there is an infinite set which is transitive for at least one color. RT²₂ is equivalent to HEM + CAC.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite set transitive for one of the colors.

statements.label: \mathsf{EM}_{<\infty}
statements.name: Erdős–Moser theorem for finitely many colors
statements.definition: Every coloring $c$ of pairs with finitely many colors has an infinite set on which it is transitive.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to k$ for some $k$.
statements.solution: An infinite set on which $c$ is transitive.

statements.label: \mathsf{fEM}_{<\infty}
statements.name: Fallow Erdős–Moser theorem for finitely many colors
statements.definition: Every coloring $c$ of pairs with finitely many colors has an infinite set on which it is fallow. Equivalent to solving finitely many instances of EM at once.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to k$ for some $k$.
statements.solution: An infinite set on which $c$ is fallow.

statements.label: \mathsf{fRT}_{<\infty}
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for fallow colorings
statements.definition: Every fallow coloring of pairs with finitely many colors has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A fallow coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to k$ for some $k$.
statements.solution: An infinite $c$-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{trRT}_{<\infty}
statements.name: Ramsey's theorem for transitive colorings, finitely many colors
statements.definition: Every transitive coloring of pairs with finitely many colors has an infinite homogeneous set. With two colors it is TRT²₂, equivalent to ADS.
statements.instance: A transitive coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to k$ for some $k$.
statements.solution: An infinite $c$-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{EM}_{\infty}
statements.name: Erdős–Moser theorem for infinitely many colors
statements.definition: Every coloring $c$ of pairs with infinitely many colors has an infinite set on which it is transitive.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to \mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite set on which $c$ is transitive.

statements.label: \mathsf{LH}
statements.name: Homogeneous subsets of limit-homogeneous sets
statements.definition: Every coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ with $\lim_y c(x, y) = 1$ for all $x$ has an infinite homogeneous set; that is, every infinite limit-homogeneous set has an infinite homogeneous subset. Uniformly computably true, yet equivalent to BΣ⁰₂ over RCA₀.
statements.instance: A coloring $c : [\mathbb{N}]^2 \to 2$ with $\lim_y c(x, y) = 1$ for every $x$.
statements.solution: An infinite $c$-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{RT}^{!\omega}_2
statements.name: Large Ramsey theorem
statements.definition: Every coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to 2$ of the exactly ω-large sets has an infinite homogeneous set.
statements.instance: A coloring $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to 2$.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-homogeneous set.

statements.label: \mathsf{FS}^{!\omega}
statements.name: Large free set theorem
statements.definition: For every $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$ there is an infinite set $H$ with $f(s) \notin H \setminus s$ for every $s \in [H]^{!\omega}$.
statements.instance: A function $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-free set.

statements.label: \mathsf{TS}^{!\omega}
statements.name: Large thin set theorem
statements.definition: For every $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$ there is an infinite set $H$ with $f([H]^{!\omega}) \neq \mathbb{N}$.
statements.instance: A function $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-thin set.

statements.label: \mathsf{RRT}^{!\omega}_2
statements.name: Large rainbow Ramsey theorem
statements.definition: For every 2-bounded $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$ there is an infinite set on which $f$ is injective.
statements.instance: A 2-bounded function $f : [\mathbb{N}]^{!\omega} \to \mathbb{N}$.
statements.solution: An infinite $f$-rainbow.

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS} + \mathsf{EM}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence + Erdős–Moser theorem

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS} + \mathsf{GP}^{2}_2 + \mathsf{WKL}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence + Grouping principle for pairs (2 colors) + Weak König's lemma

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS} + \mathsf{SCAC}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence + Stable chain–antichain principle

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS} + \mathsf{WKL}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence + Weak König's lemma

statements.label: \mathsf{ADS} + \mathsf{WWKL}
statements.name: Ascending or descending sequence + Weak weak König's lemma

statements.label: \mathsf{AMT}
statements.name: Atomic model theorem
statements.definition: Every complete atomic theory has an atomic model.
statements.instance: A complete atomic theory $T$.
statements.solution: An atomic model of $T$.

statements.label: \mathsf{ASRAM}
statements.name: Almost stable Ramsey for measure
statements.definition: For every set $X$ there is a set $Y$ such that for every martingale approximation $M \le_T X$ there is a stable coloring $f \le_T X$ on which $M$ does not succeed and which has an infinite homogeneous set $H \le_T Y$.

statements.label: \mathsf{ASRT}^{2}_2
statements.name: Almost stable Ramsey theorem for pairs (2 colors)
statements.definition: For every martingale approximation $M$ there is a stable coloring $f \le_T M$ on which $M$ does not succeed and which has an infinite homogeneous set: "non-negligibly many" stable colorings have solutions.

statements.label: \mathsf{AST}
statements.name: Atomic model theorem (subenumerable types)
statements.definition: Every complete atomic theory whose types are subenumerable has an atomic model. (A set $S$ subenumerates the types of $T$ if every type of $T$ is equivalent to $\{\varphi : \langle i,\varphi\rangle \in S\}$ for some $i$.)
statements.instance: A complete atomic theory $T$ and a set subenumerating its types.
statements.solution: An atomic model of $T$.

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Pi^0_1
statements.name: Π⁰₁ collection
statements.definition: The collection scheme for $\Pi^0_1$ formulas.

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Pi^0_2
statements.name: Π⁰₂ collection
statements.definition: The collection scheme for $\Pi^0_2$ formulas.

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2 + \mathsf{CADS}
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ collection + Cohesive ascending or descending sequence

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2 + \mathsf{CRT}^{2}_2
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ collection + Cohesive Ramsey theorem for pairs (2 colors)

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2 + \mathsf{D}^2_2 + \mathsf{WKL}
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ collection + Δ⁰₂ subset principle + Weak König's lemma

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2 + \mathsf{SADS}
statements.name: Σ⁰₂ collection + Stable ascending or descending sequence

statements.label: \mathsf{B}\Sigma^0_2 + \mathsf{SFS}^{2}
